identification.title: Before the Throne of God Above
identification.notes: Text by Charitie Lees Bancroft, 1863, and in the public domain. The tune most churches now sing is Vikki Cook's 1997 setting for Sovereign Grace, which is under copyright — so the song as sung is not public domain even though the words are.

claims.structuralNotes: Three verses, no chorus. The argument moves in order: Christ's present intercession, the answer to accusation, and the singer's standing in the risen Christ. Each verse ends by locating the singer's security outside themselves.

claims.claim: The singer has an advocate pleading for them before God's throne.
claims.subject: The intercession of Christ

claims.claim: Christ's love for the singer does not change and cannot be forfeited.
claims.subject: The unchangeable love of Christ

claims.claim: The singer's name is engraved on Christ's hands.
claims.subject: Assurance

claims.claim: When Satan accuses the singer, they look upward to Christ rather than inward.
claims.subject: The answer to accusation

claims.claim: God cannot justly punish the same sin twice, since Christ bore it already.
claims.subject: The finished atonement

claims.claim: The risen Christ is the singer's righteousness, not their own record.
claims.subject: Imputed righteousness

strengths.title: Begins where almost nothing else does
strengths.explanation: The hymn opens on Christ's present work at the throne rather than on his past work at the cross. A congregation is taught that he is doing something for them now, which is the half of his priesthood most songs never mention.
strengths.scriptureRationale: He always lives to make intercession for them — the present tense the hymn is built on.

strengths.title: Answers accusation with law, not with feeling
strengths.explanation: The second verse meets the accusing conscience by arguing that God cannot punish twice what Christ has already borne. It is a legal answer to a legal problem, which is what a despairing singer actually needs.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Who shall bring a charge against God's elect? It is Christ who died and who intercedes.

strengths.title: Names the righteousness as someone else's
strengths.explanation: The third verse says plainly that the singer's standing is Christ's record, not their own. Imputed righteousness is difficult to sing without jargon, and this manages it in a single line.
strengths.scriptureRationale: He made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

strengths.title: Security located entirely outside the singer
strengths.explanation: Every verse ends on something Christ is or has done. Sung repeatedly, the hymn trains a congregation to look away from itself for assurance, which is the habit most modern worship works against.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Your life is hidden with Christ in God — assurance that does not depend on the believer's state.

strengths.title: Holds priest, sacrifice and risen Lord together
strengths.explanation: The same Christ is advocate, offering and living Saviour across three verses without confusion. The hymn moves through his offices in order and never collapses one into another.
strengths.scriptureRationale: He entered heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf.

theological.assessment: As doctrinally dense as congregational song gets, and nothing in it is loose. It opens on Christ's present intercession rather than his past death, answers the accusing conscience with a legal argument rather than a feeling, and names the singer's righteousness as someone else's. Three verses move through his priesthood in order without confusing his offices. There is nothing here to correct.

strengths.title: An argument a congregation can follow
strengths.explanation: Three verses in a deliberate order, each ending where the singer's security actually rests. The form carries the reasoning, so a congregation learns the argument by singing it.

strengths.title: Written for the worst week
strengths.explanation: The second verse addresses someone under accusation who cannot find comfort in themselves. Very little in current use speaks to that person, and this hymn is built for them.

concerns.title: Nineteenth-century vocabulary in places
concerns.explanation: Some phrasing needs a moment from a first-time visitor. The density is the point rather than a flaw, but a leader should not assume every line lands unaided.

communal.vocalRangeNote: Vikki Cook's setting is commonly published in D and E flat. The melody is well within an ordinary room; the demand is on comprehension rather than on range.

range.key: Cook's setting commonly published in D and E flat
range.note: No chart was read for this review, so the pitches are not stated.

communal.repetitionAssessment: Almost none. Three verses of new material, which is unusual and demands more attention than a modern song — but nothing is repeated because nothing needs padding.
communal.assessment: A hymn rather than a modern song, and it asks a congregation to follow an argument rather than ride a build. That is a real demand, and worth making: the payoff is a room that has just reasoned its way through justification. The only cost is some older phrasing.

strengths.title: Each verse resolves to the same place
strengths.explanation: Every verse ends by pointing outside the singer. A hearer cannot miss where the hymn says security is found, because it says so three times in three different ways.

strengths.title: Difficult doctrine without jargon
strengths.explanation: Intercession, double jeopardy and imputation are all delivered in ordinary words. Nothing needs a footnote, and nothing is fudged to make it easier.

concerns.title: A few phrases assume some furniture
concerns.explanation: The imagery of the throne, the advocate and the graven name rewards someone who knows the Scriptures behind them. A newcomer follows the sense but may miss the argument's force.

clarity.assessment: Unusually precise. Three hard doctrines are stated in plain words without being softened, and the repeated resolution makes the hymn's claim impossible to mistake. Its only demand is a little biblical furniture, which is a fair thing for a hymn to expect.

synthesis.summary: As doctrinally dense as congregational song gets, and nothing in it is loose. It opens on Christ's present intercession rather than his past death, answers the accusing conscience with a legal argument rather than a feeling, and names the singer's righteousness as someone else's. Written for the worst week a believer will have.

scriptureReferences.relevance: Christ's present intercession, which is where the hymn chooses to begin.
The legal answer to accusation that the second verse turns into song.
The exchange the third verse names as the singer's righteousness.
A life hidden with Christ — assurance that does not rest on the believer's state.
